The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P$.

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14073156/assets/9264ecd5e62e51eec08ae686461f8b3d99aadbddd2363b5c700c72839d59524f.png)

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-12443.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
e-12443.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7).$
e-12443.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,2,7⟩-⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-12444.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
e-12444.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,2,0)$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}= \langle -4,1,1 \rangle.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=6\sqrt{2}.$
e-12444.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle + t \langle -4, 1, 1 \rangle
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩)-⟨1,2,0⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-4,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=6\sqrt{2},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{(-4t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{18{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \pm 3t\sqrt{2} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ t & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 2$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨1,2,0⟩+2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨-7,4,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨1,2,0⟩-2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨9,0,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are $A_1(-7, 4, 2)$ and $A_2(9, 0, -2).$

e-12445.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Segment
e-12445.problem: Using $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$ notation, find a parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ},$ where $P(-4,1,2)$ and $Q(-2,5,-1).$
e-12445.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(-2\,i+5\,j-k)-(-4\,i+j+2\,k) \\  & =2\,i+4\,j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{r} = (-4 \, \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\,\mathbf{k}) + t (2 \, \mathbf{i} + 4 \, \mathbf{j} - 3 \, \mathbf{k})
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(-4\,i+j+2\,k)+t(2\,i+4\,j-3\,k) \\  & =(2t-4)\,i+(4t+1)\,j+(2-3t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−3,−4,−5) and parallel to v=[1−1−2].

a
r=[−3−4−5]+[1−1−2]
b
r=[1−1−2]+t[−3−4−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−21−1]+t[−5−4−3],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[−3−4−5]+t[1−1−2],t∈(−∞,∞)
e

decision.explanation: A line through P with direction v has equation r=p+tv. Option d uses p=(-3,-4,-5) and v=(1,-1,-2); at t=0 it passes through P, and its direction is v.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-3,-4,-5)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−3,−4,−5) and parallel to v=[1−1−2].

a
r=[−3−4−5]+[1−1−2]
b
r=[1−1−2]+t[−3−4−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−21−1]+t[−5−4−3],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[−3−4−5]+t[1−1−2],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[−3−5−4]+t[1−2−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=[−3−4−5].

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=[−3−4−5]+t[1−1−2],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-3,-4,-5)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(−3,3,3) and parallel to v=⟨23,−5,3⟩.

a
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨23,−5,3⟩+t⟨−3,3,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+⟨23,−5,3⟩
d
r=⟨−5,3,23⟩+t⟨3,3,−3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨3,−3,3⟩+t⟨23,3,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: The line has equation r=q+tv. Option a uses q=⟨-3,3,3⟩, so t=0 gives Q, and its direction vector is the given v=⟨√2/3,-5,3⟩.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(-3,3,3)$ and parallel to $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨-3,3,3⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-3,3,3⟩+t⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(−3,3,3) and parallel to v=⟨23,−5,3⟩.

a
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨23,−5,3⟩+t⟨−3,3,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+⟨23,−5,3⟩
d
r=⟨−5,3,23⟩+t⟨3,3,−3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨3,−3,3⟩+t⟨23,3,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through Q and parallel to v is given by r=q+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and q is the position vector of Q.

In our case, the position vector of the point Q is q=⟨−3,3,3⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option a: r=q+tv passes through Q at t=0 and has the specified direction vector. Option c omits the parameter and describes only one point, not a line.

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(-3,3,3)$ and parallel to $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨-3,3,3⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-3,3,3⟩+t⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−1,−4,5) and parallel to v=[10−1].

a
r=[10−1]+t[−1−45],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[−1−45]+t[10−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[1−10]+t[5−4−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[−1−45]+[1−10]
e
r=[−1−45]+t[1−10],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r=p+tv with p=(-1,-4,5) and v=(1,0,-1). Option b passes through P at t=0 and has the required direction vector.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-1,-4,5)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−1,−4,5) and parallel to v=[10−1].

a
r=[10−1]+t[−1−45],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[−1−45]+t[10−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[1−10]+t[5−4−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[−1−45]+[1−10]
e
r=[−1−45]+t[1−10],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=[−1−45].

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=[−1−45]+t[10−1],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of a Line Given a Point and Direction Vector
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-1,-4,5)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

r=⟨5,35,−2⟩+t⟨2,3,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b

c

Submit

decision.explanation: A line through Q parallel to v has equation r=q+tv. Option a uses Q's position vector and the given direction v, so it passes through Q at t=0 and is parallel to v.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(\sqrt{5},\,\frac{3}{5},\,-2)$ and parallel to $v=⟨2,\,3,\,-1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$ 

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨\sqrt{5},\,\frac{3}{5},\,-2⟩.$ 

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{5},\,\frac{3}{5},\,-2⟩+t⟨2,\,3,\,-1⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 4
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(5,35,−2) and parallel to v=⟨2,3,−1⟩.

a
r=⟨5,35,−2⟩+t⟨2,3,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨2,−1,3⟩+t⟨5,−2,35⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨−2,35,5⟩+t⟨−1,2,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨2,3,−1⟩+⟨5,35,−2⟩
e
r=⟨2,3,−1⟩+t⟨5,35,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through Q and parallel to v is given by r=q+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and q is the position vector of Q.

In our case, the position vector of the point Q is q=⟨5,35,−2⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨5,35,−2⟩+t⟨2,3,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. At t=0 it gives Q=(√5,3/5,-2), and its direction vector is (2,3,-1). Option c has direction (-1,2,3), which is not parallel to the given vector.

The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$ 

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨\sqrt{5},\,\frac{3}{5},\,-2⟩.$ 

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{5},\,\frac{3}{5},\,-2⟩+t⟨2,\,3,\,-1⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(5,5,−5) and parallel to v=⟨0,−5,−1⟩.

a
r=⟨−5,5,5⟩+t⟨−1,−5,0⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨0,−1,−5⟩+t⟨5,−5,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨0,−5,−1⟩+⟨5,5,−5⟩
d
r=⟨5,5,−5⟩+t⟨0,−5,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨0,−5,−1⟩+t⟨5,5,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r=p+tv. Option d has position vector p=⟨5,5,-5⟩ and direction v=⟨0,-√5,-1⟩, so it passes through P at t=0 and is parallel to v.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(5,5,-5)$ and parallel to $v=⟨0,-\sqrt{5},-1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨5,5,-5⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨5,5,-5⟩+t⟨0,-\sqrt{5},-1⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(5,5,−5) and parallel to v=⟨0,−5,−1⟩.

a
r=⟨−5,5,5⟩+t⟨−1,−5,0⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨0,−1,−5⟩+t⟨5,−5,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨0,−5,−1⟩+⟨5,5,−5⟩
d
r=⟨5,5,−5⟩+t⟨0,−5,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨0,−5,−1⟩+t⟨5,5,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=⟨5,5,−5⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨5,5,−5⟩+t⟨0,−5,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(5,5,-5)$ and parallel to $v=⟨0,-\sqrt{5},-1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨5,5,-5⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨5,5,-5⟩+t⟨0,-\sqrt{5},-1⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points H(5,7,2) and S(3,4,5).

a
r=[572]+t[2−32],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[250]+t[−2−33],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[345]+t[−23−3],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[572]+t[−2−33],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[−2−33]+t[572],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: The direction vector is S−H=(3−5,4−7,5−2)=(-2,-3,3). Option d gives r=H+t(S−H), passing through H at t=0 and S at t=1.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $H(5,7,2)$ and $S(3,4,5).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $H$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=h+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $h$ is the position vector of $H.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $H(5,7,2)$ and $S(3,4,5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{HS} \\  & =⟨3,4,5⟩-⟨5,7,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-3,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through H and parallel to v is given by r=h+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and h is the position vector of H.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points H(5,7,2) and S(3,4,5), as follows:

v=HS→=⟨3,4,5⟩−⟨5,7,2⟩=⟨−2,−3,3⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

r=[572]+t[−2−33],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $H(5,7,2)$ and $S(3,4,5).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $H$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=h+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $h$ is the position vector of $H.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $H(5,7,2)$ and $S(3,4,5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{HS} \\  & =⟨3,4,5⟩-⟨5,7,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-3,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points C(3,2,5) and D(2,1,6).

a
r=[325]+t[−1−11],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[216]+t[1−11],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[325]+t[5311],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[316]+t[−1−11],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[325]+t[1−1−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: D−C=(2−3,1−2,6−5)=(-1,-1,1). Option a gives r=C+t(D−C), which passes through C at t=0 and D at t=1.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $C(3,2,5)$ and $D(2,1,6).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $C$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=c+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $c$ is the position vector of $C.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $C(3,2,5)$ and $D(2,1,6)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{CD} \\  & =⟨2,1,6⟩-⟨3,2,5⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points C(3,2,5) and D(2,1,6).

a
r=[325]+t[−1−11],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[216]+t[1−11],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[325]+t[5311],t∈(−∞,∞)

r=[325]+t[1−1−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through C and parallel to v is given by r=c+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and c is the position vector of C.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points C(3,2,5) and D(2,1,6), as follows:

v=CD→=⟨2,1,6⟩−⟨3,2,5⟩=⟨−1,−1,1⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

r=[325]+t[−1−11],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $C(3,2,5)$ and $D(2,1,6).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $C$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=c+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $c$ is the position vector of $C.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $C(3,2,5)$ and $D(2,1,6)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{CD} \\  & =⟨2,1,6⟩-⟨3,2,5⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(0,1,3)$ and $Q(3,-4,-2).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,1,3)$ and $Q(3,-4,-2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,-4,-2⟩-⟨0,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-5,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points P(0,1,3) and Q(3,−4,−2).

a
r=[013]+t[3−5−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[013]+t[32−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[013]+t[355],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[013]+t[−35−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[013]+t[335],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points P(0,1,3) and Q(3,−4,−2), as follows:

v=PQ→=⟨3,−4,−2⟩−⟨0,1,3⟩=⟨3,−5,−5⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

r=[013]+t[3−5−5],t∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: Q−P=(3,-5,-5), so r=P+t(Q−P) gives P at t=0 and Q at t=1. Option b has an incorrect second direction component.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(0,1,3)$ and $Q(3,-4,-2).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,1,3)$ and $Q(3,-4,-2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,-4,-2⟩-⟨0,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-5,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: B−A=(-1−4,2−5,0−3)=(-5,-3,-3). Option b gives r=A+t(B−A), passing through A at t=0 and B at t=1.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $A(4,5,3)$ and $B(-1,2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $A$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=a+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $a$ is the position vector of $A.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $A(4,5,3)$ and $B(-1,2,0)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{AB} \\  & =⟨-1,2,0⟩-⟨4,5,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,-3,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points A(4,5,3) and B(−1,2,0).

a
r=[453]+t[−120],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[453]+t[−5−3−3],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−120]+t[−5−33],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[−5−3−3]+t[453],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[533]+t[453],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through A and parallel to v is given by r=a+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and a is the position vector of A.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points A(4,5,3) and B(−1,2,0), as follows:

v=AB→=⟨−1,2,0⟩−⟨4,5,3⟩=⟨−5,−3,−3⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by r=[453]+t[−5−3−3],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $A(4,5,3)$ and $B(-1,2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $A$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=a+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $a$ is the position vector of $A.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $A(4,5,3)$ and $B(-1,2,0)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{AB} \\  & =⟨-1,2,0⟩-⟨4,5,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-5,-3,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

a
r=[431]+t[322],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[−4−3−1]+t[−353],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−4−3−1]+t[555],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[124]+t[5−55],t∈(−∞,∞)
e

decision.explanation: L−K=(1−(-4),2−(-3),4−(-1))=(5,5,5). Option c gives r=K+t(L−K), passing through K at t=0 and L at t=1.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $K$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=k+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $k$ is the position vector of $K.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{KL} \\  & =⟨1,2,4⟩-⟨-4,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨5,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through K and parallel to v is given by r=k+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and k is the position vector of K.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points K(−4,−3,−1) and L(1,2,4), as follows:

v=KL→=⟨1,2,4⟩−⟨−4,−3,−1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $K$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=k+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $k$ is the position vector of $K.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{KL} \\  & =⟨1,2,4⟩-⟨-4,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨5,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Points on the line are A=P+tv. Since |v|=√(9+4+1)=√14, the distance AP=|t|√14 equals √14 exactly when t=±1. Thus P+v=(-1,1,7) and P−v=(5,5,5), matching option c.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(2,3,6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-3,-2,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(2,3,6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-3,-2,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

provenance.kp_title: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line

history.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

decision.explanation: Points on the line are R=(1+t,t,t). Their distance from P is |t|√3, so |t|√3=3√3 gives t=±3. The two points are (4,3,3) and (-2,-3,-3), matching option b.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,0,0)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,1,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $R$ on that line such that $RP=3\sqrt{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $R$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OR} & =⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{OR}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩)-⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PR=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}RP & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PR}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,t,\,t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm t\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 3$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{R}_{1}}=⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨4,3,3⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{R}_{2}}=⟨1,0,0⟩-3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨-2,-3,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${R}_{1}(4,3,3)$ and ${R}_{2}(-2,-3,-3).$

Question 12
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(1,0,0) and is parallel to v=⟨1,1,1⟩. Find all the possible points R on that line such that RP=33.

a
R1(4,−3,−3) and R2(2,3,3)
b
R1(4,3,3) and R2(−2,−3,−3)
c
R1(4,3,3) and R2(2,3,3)
d
R1(3,4,4) and R2(3,−2,−2)
e
R1(4,2,2) and R2(−3,−2,−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since R lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OR→=⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩

and

PR→=OR→−OP→=(⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩)−⟨1,0,0⟩=t⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨t,t,t⟩.

Using the fact that PR=33, we get:

RP=33|PR→|=33|⟨t,t,t⟩|=33t2+t2+t2=333t2=33±t3=33t=±3

Finally, putting the values t=±3 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OR1→=⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨4,3,3⟩,OR2→=⟨1,0,0⟩−3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨−2,−3,−3⟩. Therefore, the points are R1(4,3,3) and R2(−2,−3,−3).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,0,0)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,1,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $R$ on that line such that $RP=3\sqrt{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $R$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OR} & =⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =\overset{\to }{OR}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,0,0⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩)-⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PR=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}RP & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PR}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,t,\,t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm t\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 3$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{R}_{1}}=⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨4,3,3⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{R}_{2}}=⟨1,0,0⟩-3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨-2,-3,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${R}_{1}(4,3,3)$ and ${R}_{2}(-2,-3,-3).$

OR1→=⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨4,3,3⟩,OR2→=⟨1,0,0⟩−3⟨1,1,1⟩=⟨−2,−3,−3⟩. Therefore, the points are R1(4,3,3) and R2(−2,−3,−3).

decision.explanation: Write Q=P+tv. Since |v|=√(1+1+25)=3√3, the distance condition gives |t|=1. Thus the only points are P+v=(2,0,6) and P−v=(0,2,-4), matching option c.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,-1,5⟩.$ Find all the possible points $Q$ on that line such that $PQ=3\sqrt{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $Q$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩)-⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PQ=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(5t)^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{27{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm 3\sqrt{3}t & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{1}}=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{2}}=⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨0,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${Q}_{1}(2,0,6)$ and ${Q}_{2}(0,2,-4).$

Question 13
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(1,1,1) and is parallel to v=⟨1,−1,5⟩. Find all the possible points Q on that line such that PQ=33.

a
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(−1,3,−9)
b
Q1(4,2,6) and Q2(1,0,2)
c
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(0,2,−4)
d
Q1(3,−1,11) and Q2(0,2,−4)
e
Q1(6,2,2) and Q2(1,0,−2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since Q lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OQ→=⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩

and

PQ→=OQ→−OP→=(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩)−⟨1,1,1⟩=t⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨t,−t,5t⟩.

Using the fact that PQ=33, we get:

PQ=33|PQ→|=33|⟨t,−t,5t⟩|=33t2+(−t)2+(5t)2=3327t2=33±33t=33t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OQ1→=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩,OQ2→=⟨1,1,1⟩−⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨0,2,−4⟩. Therefore, the points are Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(0,2,−4).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c. For Q=P+tv, the distance is |t|√27=3√3, giving t=±1. Hence the only points are (2,0,6) and (0,2,-4). Option a's second point corresponds to t=-2 and is twice the required distance away.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,-1,5⟩.$ Find all the possible points $Q$ on that line such that $PQ=3\sqrt{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $Q$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩)-⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PQ=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(5t)^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{27{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm 3\sqrt{3}t & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{1}}=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{2}}=⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨0,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${Q}_{1}(2,0,6)$ and ${Q}_{2}(0,2,-4).$

before.html:
Question 14
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,−2,3) and is parallel to v=⟨−2,1,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=3.

a
A1(1,1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
b
A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1)
c
A1(1,−1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
d
A1(1,2,5) and A2(−5,3,1)
e
A1(−1,−1,5) and A2(4,−3,−1)
Submit

decision.explanation: Points on the line have A=P+tv. Since |v|=√(4+1+4)=3, AP=3|t|=3 gives t=±1. Thus P+v=(1,-1,5) and P−v=(5,-3,1), matching option b.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,-2,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-2,1,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=3.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩)-⟨3,-2,3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=3,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =3 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =3 \\ |⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩| & =3 \\ \sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \pm 3t & =3 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩+⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨1,-1,5⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩-⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨5,-3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(1,-1,5)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,-3,1).$

Question 14
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,−2,3) and is parallel to v=⟨−2,1,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=3.

a
A1(1,1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
b
A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1)
c
A1(1,−1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
d
A1(1,2,5) and A2(−5,3,1)
e
A1(−1,−1,5) and A2(4,−3,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩)−⟨3,−2,3⟩=t⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨−2t,t,2t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=3, we get:

AP=3|PA→|=3|⟨−2t,t,2t⟩|=3(−2t)2+t2+(2t)2=34t2+t2+4t2=39t2=3±3t=3t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OA1→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨1,−1,5⟩,OA2→=⟨3,−2,3⟩−⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨5,−3,1⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,-2,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-2,1,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=3.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩)-⟨3,-2,3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=3,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =3 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =3 \\ |⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩| & =3 \\ \sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \pm 3t & =3 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩+⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨1,-1,5⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩-⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨5,-3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(1,-1,5)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,-3,1).$

OA1→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨1,−1,5⟩,OA2→=⟨3,−2,3⟩−⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨5,−3,1⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1).

Question 15
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,1,1) and is parallel to v=⟨−1,0,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=5.

a
A1(2,1,3) and A2(1,2,−1)
b
A1(2,1,3) and A2(4,1,−1)
c
A1(1,2,3) and A2(4,1,−1)
d
A1(2,1,−2) and A2(4,1,1)
e
A1(2,1,3) and A2(2,−1,1)
Submit

decision.explanation: Write A=P+tv. Since |v|=√(1+0+4)=√5, AP=|t|√5=√5 gives t=±1. Thus the only points are P+v=(2,1,3) and P−v=(4,1,-1), matching option b.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-1,0,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{5}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩)-⟨3,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-1,0,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-t,\,0,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{5},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{5} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{5} \\ |⟨-t,\,0,\,2t⟩| & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{(-t)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+0+4{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \pm \sqrt{5}t & =\sqrt{5} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,1,1⟩+⟨-1,0,2⟩=⟨2,1,3⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,1,1⟩-⟨-1,0,2⟩=⟨4,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(2,1,3)$ and ${A}_{2}(4,1,-1).$

after.html:
Question 15
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,1,1) and is parallel to v=⟨−1,0,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=5.

a
A1(2,1,3) and A2(1,2,−1)
b
A1(2,1,3) and A2(4,1,−1)
c
A1(1,2,3) and A2(4,1,−1)
d
A1(2,1,−2) and A2(4,1,1)
e
A1(2,1,3) and A2(2,−1,1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨−1,0,2⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨−1,0,2⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨−1,0,2⟩)−⟨3,1,1⟩=t⟨−1,0,2⟩=⟨−t,0,2t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=5, we get:

AP=5|PA→|=5|⟨−t,0,2t⟩|=5(−t)2+(0)2+(2t)2=5t2+0+4t2=55t2=5±5t=5t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OA1→=⟨3,1,1⟩+⟨−1,0,2⟩=⟨2,1,3⟩,OA2→=⟨3,1,1⟩−⟨−1,0,2⟩=⟨4,1,−1⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(2,1,3) and A2(4,1,−1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-1,0,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{5}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,1,1⟩+t⟨-1,0,2⟩)-⟨3,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-1,0,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-t,\,0,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{5},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{5} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{5} \\ |⟨-t,\,0,\,2t⟩| & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{(-t)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+0+4{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \pm \sqrt{5}t & =\sqrt{5} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,1,1⟩+⟨-1,0,2⟩=⟨2,1,3⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,1,1⟩-⟨-1,0,2⟩=⟨4,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(2,1,3)$ and ${A}_{2}(4,1,-1).$

before.problem:
The equation below describes all the points on the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(-3,5,0)$ and $Q(0,-3,2).$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}a \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8 \\ b\end{aligned}],\,t\in [c,1]

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
The equation below gives a parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(1,-1,1)$ and $Q(2,-3,0).$

$$
r(t)=a\,i-(2t+1)\,j+b\,k,\,t\in [c,1]
$$

What is $a+b+c?$
after.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(2\,i-3\,j)-(i-j+k) \\  & =i-2\,j-k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=(i-j+k)+t(i-2\,j-k)
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(i-j+k)+t(i-2\,j-k) \\  & =(t+1)\,i-(2t+1)\,j+(1-t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=(t+1)+(1-t)+0=2.
$$
